name: Curiosity (Mars Science Laboratory)
short_status: Operating as of 27 October 2026: fourteen years and past 5,000 Martian days, a milestone NASA's Curiosity blog dates to Saturday 29 August 2026, on a mission whose prime phase was one Martian year. The newest waypoint in NASA's MMGIS traverse file, last modified 16 October 2026, is sol 5045, a 12.64 m drive, with a cumulative drive distance of 38,480.16 m in that file's dist_total_m field, against 38.16 in the same record's dist_km field. NASA's raw images through sol 5056 (27 October 2026) show the rover at the same position.
tagline: NASA · United States · Rover · 2012 · The long occupation Operating
stats: driven across 1,386 logged waypoints from sol 3 to sol 5045, read from NASA's MSL traverse file on 28 October 2026 (last modified 16 October)
climbed above the landing site, from -4,500.97 m to -3,488.00 m on the areoid at the sol 5045 waypoint, measured from the same file on 28 October 2026
the John Klein drill hole, cut six months after landing, whose sample answered the mission's central question about ancient habitability

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 26 November 2011 at 15:02 UTC (10:02 a.m. EST) on an Atlas V 541 from Launch Complex 41, Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida. Cruise to Mars took a little over eight months.

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: 6 August 2012. The press kit predicted an Earth-received touchdown time of 05:31 UTC plus or minus a minute with a one-way light time of 13.8 minutes, which puts the actual touchdown at Mars at about 05:17 UTC, give or take a minute. JPL's event timeline of 9 August 2012 puts touchdown at 05:17:57 UTC on 6 August (10:17:57 p.m. PDT on 5 August) and the signal's arrival on Earth at 05:31:45 UTC. NSSDCA lists the landing as 05:32 UTC, which is that Earth-received time rounded to the minute. In California it was still 5 August, which is why so many sources date the landing to 5 August.

facts.label: Masses
facts.value: 3,893 kg at launch, made up of an 899 kg rover, a 2,401 kg entry, descent and landing system (aeroshell plus fuelled descent stage) and a 539 kg fuelled cruise stage. The rover is 3.0 m long not counting the arm, 2.8 m wide and 2.1 m to the top of the mast, with 0.5 m wheels and a top speed of about 4 cm per second. NSSDCA's summary box lists a single figure of 750 kg, which matches none of these and should not be quoted as the rover mass.

facts.label: Power
facts.value: One Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator holding 4.8 kg of plutonium-238 dioxide, 45 kg, 64 cm across by 66 cm long, producing slightly more than 110 W of electricity at the start of the mission, charging two lithium-ion batteries of about 42 amp-hours each. NSSDCA instead states 125 W at start of mission. The MMRTG's stated design goal was optimising power over a minimum lifetime of 14 years, a mark Curiosity passed on 6 August 2026.

facts.label: Science payload
facts.value: 75 kg in ten instruments: APXS, ChemCam, CheMin, DAN, MARDI, MAHLI, Mastcam, RAD, REMS and SAM. MEDLI, an eleventh instrument suite, measured the heat shield and atmosphere during entry only.

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: $2.5 billion as stated in the 2012 landing press kit, including $1.8 billion for spacecraft development and science investigations, with the remainder for launch and operations. That figure dates from 2012 and does not include the extended missions that began in 2014.

facts.label: Prime mission versus actual
facts.value: One Martian year, 687 Earth days, described in the press kit as 98 weeks. Sol 5056, on 27 October 2026, is about 7.6 Martian years and just over 14 Earth years after landing.

facts.label: Traverse, as measured today
facts.value: NASA's MSL_waypoints.json, read on 28 October 2026 (last modified 16 October 2026), contains 1,386 waypoints running from sol 3 to sol 5045, with a final cumulative odometry of 38,480.16 m. The same file carries a second odometry column, dist_km, which ends at 38.16 and disagrees with the metre column by about 0.32 km; that column also contains at least one clear glitch, a row at sol 3708 reading 39.37 km where the running total is 29.67 km. NASA's own public figure follows dist_km: JPL's release of 12 October 2026 credits Curiosity with more than 23.65 miles (38.07 km), the dist_km value at the sol 5021 waypoint, where the metre column reads 38,383.67 m. Earlier downloads ended sooner: at 1,384 waypoints, sol 5021 and 38,383.67 m on 9 October 2026, at 1,377 waypoints, sol 4998 and 38,176.61 m on 3 September 2026, at 1,374 waypoints, sol 4989 and 38,088.03 m on 23 August, and at 1,372 waypoints, sol 4983 and 38,015.78 m a week before that, which is where the widely repeated 38.02 km comes from.

facts.label: Elevation gained
facts.value: The traverse file's first waypoint sits at -4,500.971 m and, read on 28 October 2026, its sol 5045 waypoint at -3,487.995 m, a climb of 1,012.98 m; the highest point so far is -3,479.905 m, on sol 5021. NASA marked the kilometre of elevation gain on 26 August 2026. The lowest point on the whole traverse is -4,521.311 m, so the total ascent from the bottom of the route to the sol 5045 waypoint is about 1,033 m.

facts.label: Drill samples
facts.value: NASA's published grid of drill holes, dated 27 August 2024, shows 42 holes from John Klein (9 February 2013, sol 182) to Kings Canyon (3 August 2024, sol 4263). The team's blog for sols 5022 to 5028, posted on 4 October 2026, gives a newer count: Basque Lakes, drilled in late September 2026, is the 48th rock target the rover has drilled in Gale crater. NASA's mission page (science.nasa.gov/mission/msl-curiosity, checked 28 October 2026) still says 42.

facts.label: The habitability result
facts.value: Announced 12 March 2013. The John Klein mudstone contained at least 20 percent clay minerals by CheMin's measurement, formed in water of near-neutral pH and low salinity, and SAM identified sulfur, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and carbon. NASA's conclusion was that ancient Gale crater could have supported microbial life. It did not claim that life was there.

facts.label: Largest organics found so far
facts.value: Decane (37 plus or minus 7 pmol), undecane (41 plus or minus 8 pmol) and dodecane (19 plus or minus 4 pmol), detected by SAM in the Cumberland mudstone sample from Yellowknife Bay and published in PNAS on 24 March 2025 by Caroline Freissinet and colleagues. The authors state the origin is uncertain and could be abiotic or biological.

facts.label: Methane, as measured
facts.value: SAM's Tunable Laser Spectrometer has reported an average near 0.5 ppbv in Gale crater with occasional spikes that NASA has described as reaching about 20 ppbv; the largest single reading, in June 2019, was about 21 ppbv. ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, a far more sensitive instrument sampling the column at around 5 km altitude, has reported none. In 2021 NASA published a timing argument from John Moores of York University: TLS samples mostly at night, when the boundary layer is calm and seepage can pool near the ground, while the orbiter sees a churned daytime column. Paul Mahaffy reported that two daytime measurements matched Moores's prediction of near zero.

facts.label: Methane, proposed sources
facts.value: A NASA Goddard group led by Alexander Pavlov proposed in 2024 that methane can sit sealed under brittle perchlorate salt crusts that form in Martian regolith within three to 13 days in the lab, and that these crack under temperature swings or under the weight of a passing rover, releasing puffs. That would make some of the spikes an artefact of Curiosity's own presence rather than a global signal.

facts.label: Methane, the reliability challenge
facts.value: Viscardy, Catling and Zahnle (JGR Planets, accepted 28 March 2025) argue the spectrometer's foreoptics chamber holds methane three to four orders of magnitude above the reported sample-cell levels, that housekeeping data show unexplained pressure changes, and that leaks of under 0.1 percent of that foreoptics methane would reproduce every reported detection. They also fault the retrieval, which averages three R3-triplet lines separately instead of fitting the triplet. They propose a two-night experiment to test it. No published rebuttal from the SAM team was found as of 28 October 2026.

facts.label: Radiation
facts.value: RAD measured an average galactic-cosmic-ray dose equivalent rate of about 0.67 mSv per day on the Gale crater surface and about 1.8 mSv per day inside the spacecraft during cruise, implying roughly 0.66 Sv for the round-trip transit alone and about 1 Sv in total for a mission that adds a 500-day surface stay to that transit. Published 9 December 2013.

timeline: Launch at 15:02 UTC on an Atlas V 541 from Complex 41, Cape Canaveral, bound for Gale crater, which NASA had selected in July 2011 after a five-year process that weighed about 60 candidate sites and involved roughly 150 scientists. Total launch mass 3,893 kg, of which 899 kg is the rover itself.

Entry at about 5,900 m/s, a guided lifting entry steered by dumping tungsten ballast, a 16 m parachute at roughly 11 km, then eight throttleable rockets and the sky crane. Touchdown at about 05:17 UTC; confirmation reaches Earth around 05:31 to 05:32 UTC. MRO's HiRISE camera, aimed about a minute before touchdown, catches the spacecraft hanging under its inflated parachute in image ESP_028256_9022.

NASA names the landing spot Bradbury Landing on what would have been Ray Bradbury's 92nd birthday, and Curiosity makes its first drive the same sol (sol 16): forward about 4.5 m, a 120-degree turn, then back about 2.5 m. The traverse file logs 7.01 m of odometry for it.

On sol 182 the drill cuts its first hole, into a mudstone slab called John Klein in Yellowknife Bay, named for an MSL deputy project manager who died in 2011. JPL's release dates the drilling to 8 February in Pacific time. Five weeks later NASA announces that ancient Gale crater could have supported microbial life. Michael Meyer: 'A fundamental question for this mission is whether Mars could have supported a habitable environment. From what we know now, the answer is yes.' Day 218 of a 687-day prime mission.
Wheel damage becomes serious. The first large puncture shows up in imagery on sol 411; by sol 463 a long rip has opened. JPL slows down, drives backwards where it helps, and starts routing over sand.

NASA announces Curiosity has reached the base of Mount Sharp, the mountain it was sent to climb. Deputy project manager Jennifer Trosper notes that the wheel problem pushed the rover farther south sooner than planned.

SAM reports about 21 ppbv of methane, the largest reading of the mission. Follow-up sampling drops back below 1 ppbv. ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, in science orbit for over a year by then, has still detected none.

Three weeks that reframed the mission's chemistry. On 24 March PNAS publishes the detection of decane, undecane and dodecane in the Cumberland sample, the largest organic molecules yet found on Mars. In April, Viscardy, Catling and Zahnle publish a reanalysis in JGR Planets (accepted 28 March, announced by their institute on 14 April) arguing that Curiosity's methane detections may be instrument artefacts, and proposing a two-night experiment to settle it. On 17 April NASA reports siderite, an iron carbonate, identified by CheMin in samples from three drill sites in the sulfate-bearing layers of Mount Sharp and published in Science by Benjamin Tutolo of the University of Calgary and colleagues. NASA presents it as a possible answer to the missing-carbonate problem, and does not call it a first.

After roughly six months inside the boxwork terrain, NASA publishes close-up results on the ridges: 1 to 2 m high, crisscrossing for miles, with mineral-filled central fractures. Rice University's Tina Seeger says the groundwater table 'had to be pretty high', pushing habitable conditions later than orbital data suggested.

Curiosity drills a rock nicknamed Atacama, about 46 cm across, 15 cm thick and roughly 13 kg, and when the arm retracts the whole rock comes up with it, hanging off the fixed sleeve around the drill bit. NASA says drilling has fractured rocks before but never carried one away. Vibrating the drill does nothing, and a second try on 29 April with the arm reoriented shakes off only sand. On 1 May, tilting the drill further, rotating and vibrating it and spinning the bit frees the rock on the first round, and it breaks as it hits the ground.

NASA releases a panorama shot on sols 4930 and 4931 (19 to 20 June 2026) of Valle Grande, a valley floored with polygonal fractures 4 to 8 cm across. Project scientist Ashwin Vasavada: 'this sea of polygons took our breath away.'

Curiosity is climbing above an erosional contact on Mount Sharp, doing contact science with MAHLI and APXS, shooting ChemCam at nearby bedrock, and watching the sky for dust storms as autumn comes on. The traverse file, read the same day, records a 25.27 m drive on sol 4989 for a cumulative 38,088.03 m.

images.caption: PIA22207, a self-portrait of Curiosity standing on Vera Rubin Ridge, assembled from dozens of Mars Hand Lens Imager frames all taken on 23 January 2018, sol 1943, with the lower slopes of Aeolis Mons rising just behind the rover's mast and the rim of Gale crater on the horizon at both edges.

PIA15978, the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter catching the Mars Science Laboratory entry vehicle descending under its fully inflated parachute on 6 August 2012 UTC, with an inset cutout of the back shell stretched to avoid saturation.

The United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 rising from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral on 26 November 2011 with the Mars Science Laboratory spacecraft sealed inside its payload fairing. NASA's Kennedy Space Center media archive is the source; the file credits NASA without naming an individual photographer.
PIA16726, a Mars Hand Lens Imager view centred on the borehole Curiosity's drill cut into the mudstone slab called John Klein in Yellowknife Bay, the mission's first sample drilling on Mars.

PIA17595, a Curiosity mosaic showing the stacked geological members of the Yellowknife Bay formation and marking the two places where the rover drilled into the lowest member, Sheepbed, at the targets John Klein and Cumberland.

PIA20334, a Mars Hand Lens Imager view of Curiosity's left middle and left rear wheels, part of a routine wheel inspection set taken on 18 April 2016, sol 1315, showing punctures and tears in the aluminium skin.

PIA19142, a Curiosity self-portrait at the Mojave site on lower Aeolis Mons, combining dozens of Mars Hand Lens Imager frames taken on sols 868, 882 and 884 in January 2015, where the drill collected the mission's second sample of the mountain.
